627.  Mr Blair told the Chiefs of Staff on 15 January 2003 that “the ‘Issue’ was aftermath – the Coalition must prevent anarchy and internecine fighting breaking out”.<ref>Minute MA/DCJO to MA/CJO, 15 January 2003, ‘Briefing to Prime Minister’.</ref>

628.  In his evidence to the House of Commons Liaison Committee on 21 January 2003, Mr Blair emphasised the importance of the post‑conflict phase:
{{left margin|2em|
“You do not engage in military conflict that may produce regime change unless you are prepared to follow through and work in the aftermath of that regime change to ensure the country is stable and the people are properly looked after.”<ref>Liaison Committee, Session 2002‑2003, Minutes of Evidence Taken Before the Liaison Committee Tuesday 21 January 2003, Q 117.</ref>}}

629.  On 24 January 2003, Mr Blair told President Bush that the biggest risk they faced was internecine fighting, and that delay would allow time for working up more coherent post‑conflict plans.<ref>Letter Manning to Rice, 24 January 2003, [untitled] attaching ‘Note’.</ref>

630.  Yet when Mr Blair set out the UK’s vision for the future of Iraq in the House of Commons on 18 March 2003, no assessment had been made of whether that vision was achievable, no agreement had been reached with the US on a workable post‑conflict plan, UN authorisation had not yet been secured, and there had been no decision on the UN’s role in post‑conflict Iraq.<noinclude>{{rule|12em|align=left}}{{smallrefs}} {{rh||84|}}</noinclude>
